title: Practical: Validator Interface
story: Your signup form has three fields: age ('are you old enough?'), email ('is it valid?'), and password ('is it strong enough?'). Each needs different validation logic, but you want ONE function that validates ANY field. The Validator interface makes this clean.
why: The Validator pattern is the bridge between user input and business logic — it encapsulates validation rules behind a uniform interface, making validation composable, testable, and reusable across any input type.
analogy: Validator is like airport security — each screening station checks something different (ID validity, baggage contents, metal detection), but they all follow the same protocol: 'check this item, pass or fail.' The security system (generic function) doesn't know WHAT each station checks, only that it follows the protocol.
try_it: Add a `Username` validator (must be 3-20 chars, no spaces). Add a `PhoneNumber` validator (must be 10 digits). Create a `validate_form` function that takes a Vec of different validators (call check_field on each) and returns true only if ALL pass. What happens if you try to put Age and Email in the same Vec? (You can't — they're different types. This motivates the next section: modules and organization.)
tips: Each Validator encapsulates its OWN rules — no giant `if type == Age` switch statement needed
Include an error_message method — validation without error messages frustrates users
The validate/report pattern works for forms, APIs, configs, databases — anywhere input meets rules
common_mistakes: Building validation into the main function instead of the types — when rules change, you want to change ONE type, not every caller
Using Bool for error messages — `false` doesn't tell the user what went wrong; always include a message
Forgetting that `contains` works on Str — it's a simple check for substrings like @ and .
